source_read: PMC HTML full text PMC6450286: the publisher's version deposited by the American Medical Association (JAMA Psychiatry 2019;76(4):426-434; not an author manuscript), in its corrected form; the correction notice (JAMA Psychiatry 2019;76(4):1, PMC8177285: 413 326 'young adult', not 'adolescent', cases in the Discussion) was also read. Read in full on 2026-10-31 in the reader's own browser tab and saved as text: Key Points, Abstract, all sections, article information (funding, disclosures, correction note) and the reference list. Figures 1 to 3 were viewed on PMC's figure pages and every printed value was read from the rendered images. The article body has no table. Online supplement (eMethods 1 and 2, eTables 1 and 2) not read: per-study sample sizes, exposure definitions, adjustment sets and the risk-of-bias judgments are only there.

claims.overstatement: No overstatement of the association: 'modestly higher odds' and the association wording are more cautious than the authors' own Key Points and Conclusions. Points to fix: (1) The clause that the 7.2% attributable figure 'is not a result of its data' is not supported. The article gives no method, but the figure reproduces exactly as Levin's formula applied to the review's own pooled OR 1.37, treated as a relative risk, and the 20.9% of US adolescents reporting past-month use cited in the same paragraph: 0.209 x 0.37 / (1 + 0.209 x 0.37) = 7.18% (editors' reconstruction). Suggested wording: 'is given without a method; it matches the pooled OR treated as a relative risk combined with the share of US adolescents reporting any past-month use, although the OR compares the heaviest-use category with no use, and it assumes the link is causal.' (2) Selective qualifiers that both lean toward the null, i.e. an understatement. The claim cites the external propensity-score analysis in which the association lost significance (Harder et al.) but not the review's own propensity-score reanalysis of the Marmorstein-Iacono cohort, in which it held (OR 2.6, 1.2 to 5.5; multivariable 2.5, 1.1 to 5.5). It also says six of the 24 unpooled studies found no association without saying that the review describes most of the 24 as positive (18 cited, though one of them, ref 34, is also in the pooled set and one, ref 50, is a meta-analysis of children's peer relations). (3) Comparator: 'compared with adolescents who did not use cannabis' is the review's pooling rule (highest frequency category against non-users) for studies reporting several frequencies. For the study whose exposure is a cannabis use disorder by 17, the review does not state the comparison group.
claims.note: Every number from this source checks against the text and Figure 2: 1.37 (1.16 to 1.62), I2 0%, 7 studies; study estimates 1.44, 1.50, 1.10, 1.30, 1.48, 2.62, 1.02 (range 1.02 to 2.62), with 2 of 7 CIs excluding 1 (Brook 2002, Marmorstein 2011); 1.40 (1.17 to 1.67) without Degenhardt 2013; structured diagnosis 1.38 (1.15 to 1.66) against scales 1.28 (0.83 to 1.97); USA 1.54 (1.20 to 1.98) against other countries 1.24 (0.99 to 1.56); anxiety 1.18 (0.84 to 1.67), I2 42%, 3 studies. Countries per Figure 2: USA (2 studies), USA and Puerto Rico, Canada, UK, Australia, Australia and New Zealand, as the claim says. Recomputed DerSimonian-Laird pools from the printed rows: depression 1.37 (1.16 to 1.62); without Degenhardt 1.40 (1.18 to 1.67); structured 1.39 (1.16 to 1.67); scales 1.25 (0.79 to 1.99); USA 1.55 (1.20 to 2.00); others 1.24 (0.99 to 1.56); anxiety 1.18 (0.85 to 1.65). All match within rounding. The printed depression heterogeneity is internally inconsistent: Q = 3.26 with df 6 would give P = .78, not the printed .62; the rows give Q = 4.40 (P = .62), so the printed Q appears copied from the anxiety row (Q = 3.26, df 2, P = .20). I2 = 0% either way. 413 326 recomputed as 70 872 118 x 0.081 x 0.072 (same). The 8.1% is a 2-week prevalence in US adults aged 20 or more (ref 71), which the Discussion calls 'incidence'. 'Cannot be checked from the article' is right, and the article contradicts itself on adjustment: Statistical Analysis says all studies adjusted for prior depression and other confounders such as tobacco and alcohol; Study Selection says smoking and alcohol were controlled in 'almost all'; Limitations says not all adjusted for other drugs and cigarettes. The Narrative-review sentences (Hall & Degenhardt 2009; Hall 2015; Volkow et al. 2014) are not from this source and were not checked here.

anchors.locator: Abstract › Results; Results › Results of the Meta-analyses, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: 11 studies (23 317 individuals) in the quantitative analysis: 7 for depression, 3 for anxiety, 3 for suicidal ideation, 3 for suicide attempts. Pooled adjusted OR for depression in young adulthood, people who used cannabis in adolescence against non-users: 1.37 (95% CI 1.16 to 1.62; I2 0%). Anxiety: 1.18 (0.84 to 1.67; I2 42%), described in the Abstract as not statistically significant (but in the Results text as 'associated with increased odds').

anchors.locator: Figure 2, Depression in young adulthood rows
anchors.extracted: Adjusted ORs (95% CI): Brook 2002, USA 1.44 (1.08 to 1.91); Brook 2011, USA and Puerto Rico 1.50 (0.90 to 3.20); Degenhardt 2013, Australia 1.10 (0.60 to 1.90); Gage 2015, UK 1.30 (0.98 to 1.72); Georgiades and Boyle 2007, Canada 1.48 (0.65 to 3.40); Marmorstein and Iacono 2011, USA 2.62 (1.22 to 5.65); Silins 2014, Australia and New Zealand 1.02 (0.52 to 2.01). All above 1; only 2 of 7 intervals exclude 1. Pooled 1.37 (1.16 to 1.62); printed Q = 3.26, df = 6 (P = .62), I2 = 0% (recomputed from the rows: Q = 4.40, P = .62).

anchors.locator: Figure 2, Anxiety in young adulthood rows
anchors.extracted: Brook 2011 1.60 (0.90 to 2.90); Degenhardt 2013 1.40 (0.84 to 2.50); Gage 2015 0.96 (0.75 to 1.24); pooled 1.18 (0.84 to 1.67); Q = 3.26, df = 2 (P = .20); I2 = 42%. No study individually significant.

anchors.locator: Results › Sensitivity Analysis and Propensity Score Analysis, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Because Silins et al. 2014 includes part of the Victorian Adolescent Health Cohort used by Degenhardt et al. 2013, removing Degenhardt et al. gave a depression OR of 1.40 (95% CI 1.17 to 1.67), still significant.

anchors.locator: Methods › Study Selection, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Inclusion: peer-reviewed original articles; population-based longitudinal prospective data; cannabis-specific exposure; outcome depression, suicidal behaviour, anxiety or mixed symptoms, controlled at baseline; cannabis assessed before 18 (at least one point) and depression assessed in young adulthood (18 to 32); OR reported; adjusted for age, sex and baseline depression and/or anxiety. Parental education, socioeconomic status, alcohol and cigarette smoking controlled in almost all included studies; for a cohort reported several times, the longest follow-up was used.

anchors.locator: Methods › Parameters Definitions, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Cannabis use mostly self-reported by questionnaire; most studies reported frequency in the last year or last 6 months (weekly, daily, occasional). Where a study gave ORs for several frequency categories, only the highest category against non-users was pooled. Depression or anxiety dichotomous, by DSM-III or DSM-IV criteria or by scales with cut-offs (e.g., SCL-90, CIDI, GHQ-12, CIS-R).

anchors.locator: Results › Exploration of Heterogeneity via Meta-regression, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Depression OR with structured diagnostic tools 1.38 (1.15 to 1.66) against scales 1.28 (0.83 to 1.97), P = .74; USA 1.54 (1.20 to 1.98) against other countries 1.24 (0.99 to 1.56), P = .21; neither moderator significant.

anchors.locator: Results › Sensitivity Analysis and Propensity Score Analysis, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: The authors note that, with a modest OR, adjusting for baseline depression would not remove it as a confounder if depression is more frequent among people who use cannabis, and cite Harder et al. (ref 68), in which the OR for depression after adolescent cannabis use became non-significant with propensity-score adjusted regression.

anchors.locator: Results › Sensitivity Analysis and Propensity Score Analysis, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Reanalysis of the Marmorstein and Iacono cohort (highest depression OR in Figure 2; exposure a cannabis use disorder by age 17, outcome major depressive disorder by 24): multivariable logistic regression OR 2.5 (95% CI 1.1 to 5.5), controlling for sex, parental major depression, major depression, alcohol use disorders and nicotine dependence by 17; propensity-score method OR 2.6 (1.2 to 5.5). The association held under the review's own propensity-score analysis.

anchors.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Authors call the effect size modest and state an estimated population attributable risk of 7.2%, about 413 326 young-adult cases of depression potentially attributable to cannabis (US population aged 18 to 34 of 70 872 118 and depression 'incidence' 8.1%, the latter a 2-week prevalence in US adults aged 20 or more, ref 71). No method is given anywhere. Editors' reconstruction: Levin's formula with OR 1.37 taken as a relative risk and the 20.9% past-month-use prevalence cited in the same paragraph gives 7.18%; 70 872 118 x 0.081 x 0.072 = 413 326. Corrected on 13 March 2019 from 'adolescent' to 'young adult' cases.

anchors.locator: Discussion › Limitations, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Authors state that strong causal association cannot be made between cannabis and later depression, suicide or anxiety, because individual data were not reanalysed with causal-inference methods; not all studies adjusted for other drugs, cigarettes or psychosocial factors (refs 46, 49); depression measures varied (structured diagnosis in refs 34, 38, 44, 45, 46; symptom checklist in ref 16; a combined measure in ref 10); only frequency, not quantity, of use was available; potency has risen since 1980.

anchors.locator: Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: States that all studies reported ORs adjusted for prior depression and other confounders, giving sex, tobacco smoking and alcohol as examples, which conflicts with the Limitations; per-study adjustment sets are given only in eTable 1 of the supplement. Random-effects pooling; heterogeneity by Cochran Q and I2.

anchors.locator: Results › Systematic Review of Nonpoolable Studies and Trajectory-Based Studies, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: 24 longitudinal studies were not pooled (regression coefficients, percentages, trajectories, or same cohorts); the review says most reported a positive association between adolescent cannabis use and later depression, citing 18 references, which include ref 34 (also in the pooled depression set) and ref 50 (a meta-analysis of children's peer relations, not a cannabis cohort).

anchors.locator: Results › Systematic Review of Nonpoolable Studies and Trajectory-Based Studies, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Six studies (refs 39, 48, 55, 56, 59, 60) found no statistical association with depressive symptoms. One (ref 39) found no more depression but more anxiety at 33 in people with chronic use after controlling for baseline anxiety. Another (ref 59) supported self-medication in males, with adolescents with more depressive symptoms at baseline using more cannabis, found no link between adolescent cannabis use and later depression in either sex, and found an association between tobacco and depression.

anchors.locator: Results › Results of the Meta-analyses, 1st paragraph; Figures 2 and 3
anchors.extracted: Only adjusted odds ratios are reported; no group sizes, event counts or absolute risks for people who did and did not use cannabis appear in the article.

anchors.locator: Key Points › Findings and Meaning; Abstract › Conclusions and Relevance
anchors.extracted: Authors say the association holds even in the absence of a premorbid condition (the studies adjusted for baseline depression or anxiety; they did not exclude it), advise preadolescents and adolescents to avoid cannabis, and speak of many young people who could develop depression and suicidality attributable to cannabis: causal and advisory framing beyond an observational, adjusted association.

claims.overstatement: None for this source. Association wording; the claim itself gives the limits that matter (three studies per pool, two of three in each measured in adolescence, against the review's own criterion of young adulthood; the single young-adult ideation estimate 1.10, 0.58 to 2.07). Two further points could be added: only 1 of the 3 ideation estimates is individually significant (Weeks and Colman, a sample with no recent history of depression by its title), and the same Canadian study is in both pools. The Discussion's 'especially suicidal ideation' is the authors' wording, not used by the claim.
claims.note: All numbers check against the Abstract and Figure 3: ideation 1.50 (1.11 to 2.03), I2 0%, Q = 1.49, df = 2, P = .48; study estimates 1.40 (0.70 to 2.80, Fergusson 1996, New Zealand), 1.10 (0.58 to 2.07, McGee 2005, New Zealand, young adulthood), 1.74 (1.16 to 2.60, Weeks and Colman, Canada); attempts 3.46 (1.53 to 7.84), I2 61.3%, Q = 5.38, df = 2, P = .07; study estimates 4.81 (1.82 to 12.66, Roberts 2010, USA), 6.83 (2.04 to 22.90, Silins 2014, Australia and New Zealand, young adulthood), 1.87 (1.09 to 3.22, Weeks and Colman). Countries as the claim says. Most precise attempt estimate confirmed (log CI width: Weeks and Colman 1.08, Roberts 1.94, Silins 2.42). DerSimonian-Laird recomputation from the rows: ideation 1.50 (1.10 to 2.04), Q 1.47; attempts 3.48 (1.51 to 8.03), Q 5.39, I2 62.9%, within rounding. Weeks and Colman is dated 2016 in Figure 3 and 2017 in the reference list. The second-hand material (Hall & Degenhardt 2009; Hall 2015: case-control study, prospective studies, earlier meta-analysis) is not from this source and was not checked here.

anchors.locator: Abstract › Results
anchors.extracted: Pooled OR for suicidal ideation 1.50 (95% CI 1.11 to 2.03; I2 0%); for suicide attempt 3.46 (1.53 to 7.84; I2 61.3%).

anchors.locator: Results › Results of the Meta-analyses, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: 3 studies each for suicidal ideation and suicide attempts. Ideation: outcome measured within adolescence in refs 41 and 57 and in young adulthood in ref 47; pooled OR 1.50 (1.11 to 2.03), I2 0%. Attempts: within adolescence in refs 54 and 57, in young adulthood in ref 10; pooled OR 3.46 (1.53 to 7.84), I2 61.3%.

anchors.locator: Figure 3, Suicide ideations rows
anchors.extracted: Fergusson 1996, New Zealand 1.40 (0.70 to 2.80); McGee 2005, New Zealand 1.10 (0.58 to 2.07); Weeks and Colman 2016, Canada 1.74 (1.16 to 2.60); pooled 1.50 (1.11 to 2.03); Q = 1.49, df = 2 (P = .48); I2 = 0%. Only 1 of 3 intervals excludes 1.

anchors.locator: Figure 3, Suicide attempts rows
anchors.extracted: Roberts 2010, United States 4.81 (1.82 to 12.66); Silins 2014, Australia and New Zealand 6.83 (2.04 to 22.90); Weeks and Colman 2016, Canada 1.87 (1.09 to 3.22); pooled 3.46 (1.53 to 7.84); Q = 5.38, df = 2 (P = .07); I2 = 61.3%.

anchors.locator: Methods › Study Selection, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Inclusion requires cannabis use assessed before 18 and the outcome assessed in young adulthood (18 to 32), with ORs adjusted for age, sex and baseline depression and/or anxiety. Four of the six suicidality estimates (refs 41, 54 and 57 twice) were measured within adolescence, outside that criterion.

anchors.locator: Methods › Parameters Definitions, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Highest reported frequency category against non-users pooled where several were reported; suicide attempts and ideation assessed by questionnaires, standardized interviews or scales.

anchors.locator: Results › Results of the Meta-analyses, 1st paragraph; Figures 2 and 3
anchors.extracted: Only adjusted odds ratios are reported; no group sizes, event counts or absolute risks appear in the article.

anchors.locator: Discussion › Limitations, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Authors state that strong causal association cannot be made for depression, suicide or anxiety, and that not all studies adjusted for other drugs, cigarettes or psychosocial factors.

anchors.locator: Key Points › Findings and Meaning; Abstract › Conclusions and Relevance
anchors.extracted: Authors describe increased risk of suicidal behaviour later in life even without a premorbid condition and speak of suicidality attributable to cannabis, causal framing beyond the design; the ideation and attempt pools include outcomes measured in adolescence.

key_findings.note: Figure 1 read independently from the rendered image: same counts; databases sum to 5,076 against the printed 5,071.

Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph goes further than 'almost all': it says all studies reported ORs adjusted for prior depression and other confounders, giving sex, tobacco smoking and alcohol as examples. The finding could record both statements (see missed).

All seven estimates match this reader's reading of Figure 2. In the note, 'against no use' holds by the review's stated rule for studies reporting several frequency categories; for the cannabis use disorder study the article does not state the comparison group.
Recalculation reproduced: random effects 3.48 (1.51 to 8.03), tau-squared 0.341; fixed effect 2.70 (1.74 to 4.19).
Recalculation without Marmorstein and Iacono reproduced: 1.33 (1.12 to 1.58), tau-squared 0.

Including the trajectory study of 1,232 college students, the two studies on stopping by the end of adolescence, the 5-HTTLPR study and the Degenhardt 2013 citation (continued use to 29) against its pooled 1.10.
Reconstruction reproduced independently in step 1: 0.209 x 0.37 / (1 + 0.209 x 0.37) = 7.18%; 70,872,118 x 0.081 x 0.072 = 413,326.

reporting_issues.note: Found independently: recomputed depression Q 4.40 (P = .62); Q 3.26 with 6 df gives P = .78; anxiety recomputed Q 3.44, I2 41.9%.
Introduction, 5th paragraph: '18 years and younger'; Methods › Study Selection: younger than 18. Four of the six suicidality estimates were measured in adolescence.
Refs 34, 49 and 50 as stated; ref 50 is in both the list of 35 and the list of 18 positive non-pooled studies.

There is a third, stronger statement: Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph says all studies reported ORs adjusted for prior depression and other confounders, e.g., sex, tobacco smoking and alcohol. Adding it would make the inconsistency complete (all / almost all / not all).

risk_of_bias.note: Overall critically low agreed: items 2, 4 (under senior decision 21) and 15 fail on their own. Single-domain differences: item 13 'no' is a close call that this reader would judge 'yes' by the item's wording, because the Limitations and the 2nd paragraph of Results › Sensitivity Analysis discuss the likely effect of confounding (incomplete adjustment for drugs, tobacco and psychosocial factors; residual confounding by depression), even though the Key Points and Conclusions ignore it. Item 9 'partial-yes' is defensible; the RTI item bank covers confounding, selection, measurement and reporting, so the technique alone would meet 'yes', and the missing ratings bear on items 12 and 13. One wording point in the reasoning: 'the attributable-case figure is not a result of the review's data' conflicts with the card's own key finding 12 and interpretation_gap point 2, which show the figure applies the pooled OR, as a relative risk, to an outside prevalence. 'Is not a finding of the review' would be exact. Provisional, because the supplement was not read.

interpretation_gap.note: 'Substantial' is right. Points 1 to 7 are all borne out by the text and Figures 1 to 3 as read by this reader.

missed: Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph states that all studies reported ORs adjusted for prior depression and other confounders, e.g., sex, tobacco smoking and alcohol. This is the strongest of three inconsistent statements on adjustment (Study Selection: 'almost all'; Limitations: 'not all'); add it to reporting issue 9 and key finding 2.

Comparator for the cannabis use disorder study: the review pools the highest frequency category against non-users only for studies that reported several categories. For Marmorstein and Iacono (exposure a cannabis use disorder by 17), the article does not say who the comparison group was, so 'against no use' (design_detail, comparison.controls, key finding 4 note) is not established for that study.

Wording carried into claim cl_can_teen_depression_anxiety: the risk_of_bias reasoning's 'not a result of the review's data' became the claim's 'is not a result of its data'. Both should follow key finding 12: no stated method; it applies the pooled OR, treated as a relative risk, to the share of US adolescents with any past-month use; it assumes causation.
Minor: Weeks and Colman are dated 2016 in Figure 3 but 2017 in the reference list (ref 57); the card follows the figure.
